channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today's ranked reading list collects five relevance-3 skims at the application and tooling edge of quantum computing: 2611.08151 on an ML surrogate for hybrid quantum Monte Carlo, 2611.08220 on differential testing for quantum software stacks, 2611.09873 on trajectory-dependent decoherence and leakage in shuttled multi-spin qubits, 2611.09659 on an OpenQASM3-to-QuEST compiler and HPC-quantum offload model, and 2611.09779 on differentiable digital twins for calibration and characterization of neutral-atom and trapped-ion systems; together they inform workflow acceleration, compiler validation, scaling theory, HPC integration, and calibration methodology, though none directly addresses operation or benchmarking of the current static 16-qubit spin-qubit QPU. No pay dirt today — 3 to skim.

item.title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
item.description:
Skim new method — Machine-learning surrogates compress quantum randomized-measurement data to bypass classical shadow postprocessing, enabling chemically accurate quantum-classical QMC on up to 40 qubits with 190-fold to 4,100-fold speedups.

Grade 0.564 · 3.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computers for High-Performance Computing”

Figure

Energy error relative to infinite-shot reference versus qubit count (8 to 40 qubits) for hydrogen chains (b), and total classical CPU/GPU cost for brute-force shadow processing versus ML surrogate showing 190- to 4,100-fold speedups (c).

Asks

How can the computational bottleneck of repeatedly reconstructing quantum trial-state overlaps from classical shadows during quantum Monte Carlo propagation be overcome?

Before

Hardware demonstrations of quantum-classical QMC were limited to 16 qubits and required over 13,000 GPU hours for a single calculation; 40-qubit postprocessing was estimated to take millions of CPU hours.

But

Requires training determinants Ntrain≪NwNτ; training stopped via experimental noise floor F to avoid overfitting finite measurement noise.

Tools

Google Willow processor · auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) · Clifford matchgate classical shadows · neural quantum states (NQS) · nonorthogonal configuration interaction (NOCI)

Abstract

Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

item.title: Quantum Integration Software Suite For HPC-Quantum Computing Workflows
item.description:
Skim new method — Introduces QASC, translating OpenQASM3.0 classical control and circuits into C++ linked to QuEST, plus QACC-perf, which estimates HPC-QPU offloading communication latencies ranging from 0.084 ms on-node to 2718.000 ms over cloud across molecular circuits up to 50.3 MB.

Grade 0.686 · 5.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Integration of Quantum Accelerators with High Performance Computing—A Review of…” · Mateusz Meller, Joseph C. R. Thacker, Thomas W. Keal, Vendel Szeremi

Figure

Communication overhead in ms against circuit size in MB across on-node, multi-node, and cloud integration modes, alongside transpilation-to-execution runtime ratios across tested molecular system sizes.

Asks

How can OpenQASM3.0 programs with complex classical control be efficiently simulated and their HPC–quantum computing integration performance quantitatively modelled?

But

Does not support OpenQASM3.0 gate calibration, physical qubits, pragmas, or annotations; performance model tested via simulation rather than physical QPU hardware.

Tools

QASC (Quantum Assembly Compiler) · QuEST simulator · QACC-perf performance model · ChemShell · Antlr4

Code. https://github.com/stfc/QASC

Abstract

In this work, we focus on addressing challenges related to modelling the integration of conventional high-performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing (QC). We introduce the Quantum Assembly Compiler (QASC) for OpenQASM3.0 files. The compiler produces an executable that leverages the high-performance simulator QuEST to simulate quantum programs. Additionally, we introduce a performance modelling tool, QACC-perf, which can estimate the cost of integrating QC in classical HPC workflows, as well as the execution time of the quantum circuits. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these tools in the context of multiscale quantum chemistry workflows using the ChemShell computational chemistry environment.

item.title: Differentiable Digital Twins for Optimization, Calibration, and Characterization of Neutral-Atom- and Ion-based Quantum Computers
item.description:
Skim new method — Introduced differentiable-digital-twin software framework `qruise-toolset` for atomic qubits, simulating single-qubit randomized benchmarking with error per Clifford of 1.11(30)×10−3 and achieving quantum volume of 24=16 with 83.1% mean heavy-output probability.

Grade 0.554 · 3.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Integration of Quantum Accelerators with High Performance Computing—A Review of…” · Marco Rossignolo, Lorena C. Bianchet, Anurag Saha Roy, Shai Machnes

Figure

Heavy-output probability per circuit for 200 random four-qubit square circuits of depth 4. The cumulative mean (solid line) stays at 83.1%, exceeding the 2/3 pass threshold (dashed line) to demonstrate a quantum volume of 16.

Asks

How can atomic quantum processor dynamics and hardware control stacks be modelled and calibrated using end-to-end automatic differentiation?

But

Demonstrated primarily in numerical simulation; subject to exponential resource scaling for full state and process tomography.

Tools

automatic differentiation · quantum optimal control · digital twin modeling · Qiskit backend emulation · randomized benchmarking

Abstract

Quantum technologies based on individually controlled atoms are among the most promising platforms for scalable quantum computing, owing to their favorable coherence properties and controllability. Nonetheless, achieving reliable and high-fidelity gate operations remains challenging due to the sensitivity of these systems to noise and hardware imperfections. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive software toolset designed to model atomic quantum systems with high precision and simulate qubit gate dynamics. By integrating quantum optimal control and benchmarking techniques with automatic differentiation for efficient and accurate gradient-based optimization, the toolset enables significant improvements in gate performance. We demonstrate its capabilities through detailed case studies involving both neutral atoms and trapped ions, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing quantum gate fidelities, and providing valuable insights for experimental implementation.
